prompt: A server you have just inherited needs hardening. What does this course do first?

choices.text: Install an endpoint protection product on it
choices.why: A control protects what is there; first find out what is there.

choices.text: Measure what it exposes
choices.why: Right: measure, change, measure again.

choices.text: Reinstall it from a clean image before looking at anything
choices.why: Reinstalling throws away the answer to what the machine was doing and for whom.

choices.text: Change every password on it, starting with root's
choices.why: Useful later, and it misses the services and the second root.

prompt: Which command answers, in one line per account, who on a Linux machine is root?

choices.text: getent group sudo
choices.why: That lists who may use sudo, not who is user id 0.

choices.text: grep root /etc/passwd
choices.why: It finds the name root, and misses a second root with another name.

choices.text: awk -F: '$3 == 0' /etc/passwd
choices.why: Right: the kernel checks the number, so the question is about the number.

choices.text: sudo passwd -S -a
choices.why: That reports password states, not user ids.

prompt: A port is still open after its service was stopped and disabled, and ss names systemd as the holder. What is the fix?

choices.text: Disable the matching .socket unit as well
choices.why: Right: socket activation lets systemd listen for the service.

choices.text: Restart systemd so that it lets go of the port
choices.why: systemd would listen again at once, because the socket is still enabled.

choices.text: Block the port in the network firewall in front of the server
choices.why: That hides the listener from some clients and leaves it on the machine.

choices.text: Wait: the kernel releases a closed port after a timeout
choices.why: Nothing is closing; systemd is listening on purpose.

prompt: Two drop-in files set PasswordAuthentication: 20-a.conf says no and 60-b.conf says yes. What does sshd do?

choices.text: Accepts passwords, because the later file overrides the earlier one
choices.why: That is how most programs work, and not sshd.

choices.text: Refuses to start, because the two values conflict
choices.why: Repeating a keyword is valid; sshd -t passes.

choices.text: Refuses passwords
choices.why: Right: sshd keeps the first value it reads, and 20 is read before 60.

prompt: A scan found ports 21, 22, 23, 80 and 111 open over TCP on a portal whose job needs SSH and HTTP. How many TCP ports should the scan show after hardening?
Which statements about switching a service off are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A masked unit cannot be started, even by a unit that depends on it
choices.why: It is linked to /dev/null.

choices.text: A disabled unit can no longer be started by hand
choices.why: disable only removes it from boot; systemctl start still works.

choices.text: A purged package leaves no configuration file behind
choices.why: That is the difference between purge and remove.

choices.text: Masking a service also removes its binary from disk
choices.why: The binary stays, and keeps getting updated.

prompt: Which CIS profile is meant to be safe to apply to any server without losing a function?

choices.text: Level 2 Server, because it is the stricter of the two
choices.why: Stricter is exactly why it may cost a function.

choices.text: Level 1
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The STIG profile, which every guide derives from
choices.why: STIGs are a separate, stricter source.

choices.text: The Standard profile of the vendor's own guide
choices.why: That is SSG's profile name, not a CIS level.

prompt: Why keep the check that proves a baseline separate from the playbook that applies it?

choices.text: Because Ansible cannot run shell commands on the target machine
choices.why: It can; the reason is what each one can see.

choices.text: Because checks must run as root and playbooks must not
choices.why: The playbook runs with become: true as well.

choices.text: A playbook reports what it changed; a check reports what is true
choices.why: Right. Drift in a file the playbook does not own is invisible to it.

choices.text: To keep the baseline secret from the administrators who run Ansible
choices.why: Nothing about a baseline is secret from the people who apply it.

prompt: A scanner evaluates a guide written for Ubuntu 22.04 against a 24.04 server and every rule comes back not applicable. What is the right next step?

choices.text: Edit the guide's platform names so the rules run
choices.why: The results would look real and mean nothing.

choices.text: Report the server as compliant, since no rule failed
choices.why: No rule passed either: nothing was tested.

choices.text: Get content for 24.04, or write the checks yourself
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Downgrade the server to 22.04 so that the guide applies
choices.why: Changing the system to fit an audit tool is backwards.

prompt: What turns a documented exception into a permanent weakness?

choices.text: Having no expiry date
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Having been approved by the administrator rather than a manager
choices.why: Who approves matters less than whether it is ever reviewed.

choices.text: Being recorded in a Lynis profile with skip-test
choices.why: Recording it is good; the reason and expiry are what is missing.

choices.text: Having a compensating control that covers the risk
choices.why: That is what makes an exception acceptable.

prompt: Put the parts of a CIS recommendation in the order an administrator uses them.
items: read the rationale to decide whether it fits
check the impact for what may stop working
run the audit to see whether the machine complies
apply the remediation

prompt: A playbook is run a second time on a machine it has already brought into line. If it is idempotent, how many changes does the recap report?
Which command shows what Group Policy actually applied on a Windows machine, and from which GPO?

choices.text: gpupdate /force
choices.why: That asks for a refresh; it does not report.

choices.text: gpresult /r, or /h for the full report
choices.why: Right: the resultant set of policy.

choices.text: secedit /export
choices.why: That dumps local security settings, without the GPO each came from.

choices.text: reg query on the policy key
choices.why: It shows values, not which GPO set them.

prompt: A domain-joined computer's local policy sets a password length of 8 and the domain baseline sets 14. Which applies?

choices.why: Right. Local is processed first and overwritten.

choices.text: 8, because the machine's own setting is the most specific
choices.why: That is Ansible's rule for host variables, not Group Policy's.

choices.text: Whichever was changed most recently
choices.why: Order decides, not dates.

choices.text: Neither: the conflict disables the setting until resolved
choices.why: There is no conflict state; the last one processed wins.

prompt: What turns a configuration tool such as Ansible into an audit tool without changing any machine?

choices.text: Running it as a user without sudo so it cannot write
choices.why: Tasks would fail rather than report a difference.

choices.text: Check mode with a diff
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Removing the handlers from the playbook so nothing restarts
choices.why: The tasks would still change files.

choices.text: Pointing it at an empty inventory first
choices.why: Then it compares nothing at all.

prompt: A playbook manages only the SSH drop-in file. Which drift would its check mode miss? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A new drop-in file that sorts before it
choices.why: Not managed, so not compared.

choices.text: A hand edit inside the file it manages
choices.why: That is exactly what it reports.

choices.text: A package installed by hand
choices.why: No task looks at packages.

choices.text: A second account with user id 0
choices.why: No task looks at accounts.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a new baseline GPO before a machine applies it.
items: the settings are written into a GPO
the GPO is linked to an OU
the machine refreshes in the background
gpresult shows the GPO as applied

prompt: In an Ansible inventory, where does a value that only one machine should have belong?

choices.text: In group_vars/all.yml, with a comment naming the machine
choices.why: all.yml applies to every machine.

choices.text: In host_vars/<machine>.yml
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In the playbook, inside an if around the task
choices.why: That hides a declared difference inside the logic.

choices.text: In the systemd unit that runs the playbook on a timer
choices.why: The unit only runs the playbook; it holds no values.

prompt: Why is MAC filtering a convenience control rather than an access control?

choices.text: Because MAC addresses change every time a device reboots
choices.why: They stay fixed unless somebody changes them.

choices.text: The device writes its own address
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because switches can store only a few addresses per port
choices.why: Capacity is not the weakness.

choices.text: Because MAC filtering slows every frame down noticeably
choices.why: It is cheap, which is its merit.

prompt: In 802.1X, which party decides whether a device may join?

choices.text: The supplicant, after checking the server's certificate
choices.why: It checks the server; it does not decide its own access.

choices.text: The switch port, by comparing the MAC with its list
choices.why: That is MAC filtering, not 802.1X.

choices.text: The authentication server, behind the switch
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The DHCP server, by giving or withholding an address
choices.why: DHCP comes after the port opens.

prompt: What makes EAP-TLS stronger than PEAP with a password?

choices.text: No password exists to guess or phish
choices.why: Right: a key the network signed.

choices.text: It encrypts the traffic after login, which PEAP does not
choices.why: Neither encrypts wired traffic after login.

choices.text: It runs without any certificate authority
choices.why: It needs one more than PEAP does.

choices.text: It lets the switch skip asking the RADIUS server
choices.why: The server still decides.

prompt: Which are sound outcomes for devices that fail or skip 802.1X? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A guest VLAN with internet and no internal route
choices.why: For devices that do not speak 802.1X.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the login conversation
choices.why: The safe default.

choices.text: The staff VLAN, logged for later review
choices.why: Logging is not restricting.

choices.text: A printers-only segment for a MAC-authenticated printer
choices.why: Limited to what a printer needs.

prompt: Put the life of an 802.1X port in order.
items: unauthorised: only EAPOL passes
the device completes EAP with the server
authorised: the device's traffic flows
logoff: the port closes again

prompt: A NAC server admits a known laptop but places it in a remediation network. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Its certificate is signed by an unknown authority
choices.why: Then it would not have been admitted as known.

choices.text: Its posture failed, for example missing updates
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Its MAC address appeared on two ports
choices.why: That is a switch alert, not a posture result.

choices.text: It logged in during a guest's session on the same socket
choices.why: Sessions on a port do not overlap like that.

prompt: On Ubuntu, what makes an nftables rule set survive a reboot?

choices.text: Loading it with nft -f once
choices.why: That changes only the running kernel.

choices.text: /etc/nftables.conf with nftables.service enabled
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Saving it with nft -c before the reboot
choices.why: -c only checks.

choices.text: Adding the counter keyword to every rule
choices.why: Counters count; they do not persist anything.

prompt: Which answer suits a port on an address the internet can reach, and why?

choices.text: Drop: a scan is slower and learns less
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Reject: the scanner gives up and never comes back
choices.why: A refusal is an answer, and scanners return.

choices.text: Drop: it makes the machine invisible on every other port too
choices.why: A host that answers on one port is a host.

choices.text: Reject: it uses less bandwidth than silence
choices.why: Silence sends nothing at all.

prompt: Why keep both the purge of unneeded services and a default-deny firewall?

choices.text: Because a firewall cannot block ports below 1024
choices.why: It blocks any port.

choices.text: Each covers what the other misses
choices.why: Right: today's flaws and tomorrow's listeners.

choices.text: Because CIS requires two controls for every risk
choices.why: No such rule; the reason is coverage.

choices.text: Because a purged service comes back after every reboot
choices.why: Purged is gone; the lab's up resets it, a real server does not.

prompt: Which USB risks does a device allow-list that checks interfaces address? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An unknown stick from the car park
choices.why: Not on the list.

choices.text: A stick that also presents a keyboard
choices.why: Interfaces must match.

choices.text: Malware on an allowed stick
choices.why: The stick is allowed; its files are another control's job.

choices.text: A device built to copy an allowed one's ids
choices.why: Ids are self-reported.

prompt: Put the rules of the portal's input chain in the order they appear.
items: accept the loopback
accept established and related
drop invalid
accept HTTP from anybody
accept SSH from admin and jump

prompt: What should be open before you load a new firewall on a remote server?

choices.text: A browser tab on the server's web page
choices.why: That does not get you back in.

choices.text: Every port, until the rules are tested
choices.why: That is no firewall at all.

choices.text: A second session, or a console
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A ticket with the hosting provider
choices.why: Useful after a lockout, not instead of avoiding one.

prompt: Which command lists every regular file on the root file system that any user may write?

choices.text: find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000
choices.why: That finds set-user-id files.

choices.text: find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002
choices.why: Right: the other-write bit.

choices.text: ls -l / | grep rwx
choices.why: It lists one directory, and rwx matches owners too.

choices.text: getfacl -R / | grep other
choices.why: It prints every other entry, writable or not.

prompt: Why can `chmod g-w` on a file with an ACL remove write access from a named user?

choices.text: On an ACL file the group bits are the mask
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because chmod deletes named entries it does not recognise
choices.why: The entries stay; the mask caps them.

choices.text: Because named users are always members of the owning group
choices.why: They need not be.

choices.text: Because g-w is applied to every group on the system
choices.why: It changes one file's bits.

prompt: What does a default ACL on a directory grant on the directory itself?

choices.text: The same entries it gives new files
choices.why: It is a template, not access.

choices.text: Read to everybody named in it
choices.why: It grants nothing on the directory.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Full control to the directory's owner
choices.why: The owner's access comes from the bits.

prompt: Where does most of an NTFS file system's access usually come from?

choices.text: From entries written on each file one by one
choices.why: Most are not written on the file.

choices.text: From inheritance down from parent folders
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: From the nine permission bits underneath
choices.why: NTFS has no bits underneath.

choices.text: From the user's group membership alone, with no lists
choices.why: Every object has a list.

prompt: Which files must not be writable by accounts with less privilege than the program that uses them? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A script in /etc/cron.d run as root
choices.why: Root runs whatever it says.

choices.text: A systemd unit file of a root service
choices.why: It decides what root starts.

choices.text: A client's tax document read by the auditor
choices.why: Confidential, but nothing runs it with privilege.

choices.text: The directory holding /etc/sudoers.d
choices.why: A new file there changes sudo.

prompt: Put the questions Linux asks of a POSIX ACL in order.
items: is this the owner?
is there an entry with this user's name?
does one of this user's groups appear?
otherwise, what does other allow?

prompt: A file differs from a known bad one in a single byte. Which signature can still match it?

choices.text: A SHA-256 hash signature of the known file
choices.why: Any byte changes the hash.

choices.text: A content signature for bytes both still share
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: An MD5 hash signature, because MD5 is weaker
choices.why: Weak against collisions, still exact to the byte.

choices.text: None: one byte makes it a different file to any scanner
choices.why: Only to a hash.

prompt: After changing the mail gateway's policy, how do you check its scanner still works, without real malware?

choices.text: Send it the EICAR test file
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Wait for the next real detection in the logs
choices.why: That could take weeks and proves nothing now.

choices.text: Read the policy file again carefully
choices.why: A claim until a file has been caught.

choices.text: Turn off quarantine so detections are visible
choices.why: That weakens it.

prompt: Why is deleting on detection worse than quarantine when heuristics are enabled?

choices.text: Because deletion is slower than moving a file
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Because quarantined files are scanned again until clean
choices.why: They are held, not cleaned.

choices.text: Some detections are wrong, and deletion cannot be undone
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because heuristics refuse to run when deletion is set
choices.why: They run either way.

prompt: Which of these does a file scanner miss by design? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A file nobody has described yet
choices.why: No signature exists.

choices.text: Commands run with tools already installed
choices.why: No bad file.

choices.text: An exact copy of a file on its hash list
choices.why: That is what it catches best.

choices.text: An intruder using a stolen password
choices.why: Nothing malicious to scan.

prompt: Put the parts of a YARA rule in the order they are written.
items: rule and its name
strings: the patterns
condition: how they combine

prompt: Which monitoring check catches a scanner that quietly stopped protecting, while still reporting clean?

choices.text: Whether the scanner process is running
choices.why: It runs, with old signatures.

choices.text: The age of the signature database
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The number of files scanned last night
choices.why: It scans as many as ever.

choices.text: The size of the quarantine directory
choices.why: An empty quarantine looks like good news.

prompt: A script that never writes to disk runs on a server. Which tool has a chance of noticing it?

choices.text: An antivirus that scans every file written to the disk
choices.why: Nothing is written, so there is nothing to scan.

choices.text: An EDR watching processes
choices.why: Right: it judges what runs, not what is stored.

choices.text: A vulnerability scanner run once a week against the server
choices.why: It reports missing patches, not what is running now.

choices.text: The file integrity checker, comparing hashes of system files
choices.why: No file changed.

prompt: Which single field of process telemetry most often turns an ordinary program into an alert?

choices.text: Its parent chain
choices.why: Right: bash is normal; bash under the web server is not.

choices.text: The size of the program file on disk
choices.why: Size says nothing about why it ran.

choices.text: The process id the kernel gave it
choices.why: Ids are handed out in order and mean nothing alone.

choices.text: How much memory it used in its first second of life
choices.why: A resource figure, not a behaviour.

prompt: Order the response to a suspicious process on a server.
items: record its program hash and environment
stop the process
isolate the machine, leaving the responders' access
rebuild or restore the machine

prompt: A sensor polls the process list every second. Which activity is it most likely to miss?

choices.text: A reverse shell that stays connected for an hour
choices.why: It lives across thousands of looks.

choices.text: A web server worker that runs all day
choices.why: Long-lived processes are the easy case.

choices.text: A one-line command that copies a file and exits
choices.why: Right: it can start and end between two looks.

choices.text: A cron job that sleeps for five minutes before working
choices.why: Sleeping keeps it alive across many looks.

prompt: What does tamper protection in an EDR product defend against?

choices.text: Malware hiding inside compressed archives
choices.why: That is the scanner's business.

choices.text: Somebody with root stopping or removing the agent
choices.why: Right: and an agent that falls silent is itself an alert.

choices.text: Users changing their own passwords too often
choices.why: Nothing to do with the agent.

choices.text: Network packets altered on their way to the console
choices.why: Transport encryption covers that, not tamper protection.

prompt: On Linux, small programs that the kernel verifies and then runs at chosen points, used by modern sensors, are called ___.
Data being pasted into a browser from an open spreadsheet is in which state, and where can it be watched?

choices.text: At rest, by a scan of the file server
choices.why: The file server never sees a paste.

choices.text: In use, on the endpoint
choices.why: Right: only an agent there sees the action.

choices.text: In motion, at the network edge, before it is encrypted
choices.why: By the time it crosses the edge it is encrypted.

choices.text: At rest, by the mail gateway reading attachments
choices.why: No mail is involved.

prompt: A scanner validates CPF check digits and still reports an invoice number. What is the most useful next step?

choices.why: That would multiply the false positives.

choices.text: Report the invoice number to the ANPD as a leaked CPF
choices.why: It is not anybody's CPF in that file.

choices.text: Add context or a count threshold to the rule
choices.why: Right: those reduce what the arithmetic cannot.

choices.text: Delete the invoice file so the alert stops
choices.why: The invoice is legitimate data the firm needs.

prompt: Why should a DLP tool's alerts mask the numbers they found?

choices.why: Right: into logs, tickets and mail.

choices.text: Because full numbers make the alerts too long to read
choices.why: Length is not the reason.

choices.text: Because masked numbers are easier to search for later
choices.why: They are harder to search, on purpose.

choices.text: Because the check digits are only valid when masked
choices.why: Masking does not change validity.

prompt: A new DLP rule is about to go live. What should it do in its first weeks?

choices.why: It would stop legitimate work and be switched off.

prompt: A card number reads 9999 8797 3091 141? with the last digit missing. Using Luhn's rule, what must the last digit be?
Which of these are LGPD principles the lesson ties to DLP? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Necessity
choices.why: Hold only what the purpose needs.

choices.text: Security
choices.why: Technical and administrative measures to protect the data.

choices.text: Anonymity of the controller
choices.why: No such principle exists.

choices.text: Free circulation of data between companies
choices.why: Not a principle of the law.

prompt: Which traffic does a host firewall see that a firewall between segments never does?

choices.text: Traffic from the internet to the firm's public web site

choices.text: Encrypted traffic to cloud services

choices.text: DNS queries to the internet's root servers

prompt: Why is outbound filtering worth more on a server than on a workstation?

choices.why: That is not the argument.

choices.text: Its few destinations can be listed, so anything else is a signal

choices.text: Workstations have no outbound traffic worth filtering

choices.text: Servers have no inbound rules to rely on
choices.why: They do; lesson 5 wrote some.

prompt: A drop-in sets IPAddressDeny=any for a service, and systemctl show prints it. What still has to be done before relying on it?

choices.why: This lesson showed it printed and did nothing.

choices.text: Add the same rule to the network firewall

prompt: Which nftables feature shows the rule that decided a particular packet's fate?

choices.text: nft list ruleset -a

prompt: Match each way of naming a program in a rule to where it is written.

choices.why: That is the inbound default.

choices.text: Allows it unless a rule blocks it

choices.text: Asks the user for each new program

choices.text: Allows it only on the Domain profile

prompt: A rule flags every login outside office hours. Should it block or alert?

prompt: After changing a fail2ban jail, what is the one test that proves it works?

choices.text: Read jail.conf to see the defaults

prompt: What makes a file integrity database worth trusting?

choices.why: A nightly rebuild approves every change unread.

choices.text: Built on a known-good machine, approved by a person, kept off it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Covering every file on the disk, including logs

choices.text: Using the strongest hash available

prompt: What can mandatory access control stop that file permissions cannot?

choices.text: A program using rights its account has but its job does not need
choices.why: Right: confinement is per program.

choices.text: Root changing the owner of a file
